sec.title: Purpose:
sec.p: Gastrointestinal tumors, including esophageal and gastric/gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma (GEA), have a high mortality rate and present significant treatment challenges. Telisotuzumab adizutecan (Temab-A, ABBV-400), a novel antibody–drug conjugate targeting the c-Met protein (also known as MET protein), has shown encouraging results in patients with advanced GEA.

sec.title: Patients and Methods:
sec.p: This phase I, open-label, multicenter study assessed the safety, efficacy, and pharmacokinetics (PK) of Temab-A monotherapy (3 mg/kg every 3 weeks intravenously) in patients with advanced GEA. Patients ≥18 years of age with advanced/metastatic GEA who had received 1 to 2 prior systemic therapies were included. The primary objectives were the evaluation of safety, PK, and efficacy; efficacy endpoints included objective response rate (ORR), duration of response (DOR), progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS). c-Met expression and MET amplification were retrospectively assessed.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Forty-two patients with advanced GEA were enrolled; the median age was 60 years. The median follow-up duration was 12.6 months. All patients had one or more treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAE), with 88% experiencing grade ≥3 TEAEs. The most common hematologic TEAEs were anemia (67%), nausea (52%), and decreased appetite (36%). The ORR was 29%, the clinical benefit rate was 71%, and the median DOR was 4.2 months. The median PFS was 4 months, and the median OS was 5.8 months. Exploratory biomarker analyses showed ORR enrichment in patients with higher c-Met protein expression and MET focal amplification.

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: Temab-A monotherapy demonstrated antitumor activity and a manageable safety profile in patients with advanced GEA. The findings support further clinical development of Temab-A, particularly in combination with other agents to improve outcomes for patients with 2L+ GEA.

boxed-text.p: Patients with advanced gastric/gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma (GEA) face limited treatment options and poor survival outcomes, particularly after progression on standard therapies. This study evaluates telisotuzumab adizutecan (Temab-A, ABBV-400), a novel antibody–drug conjugate (ADC) targeting the c-Met protein (also known as MET protein), in a heavily pretreated GEA population. Temab-A demonstrated antitumor activity with a manageable safety profile, including in patients with high c-Met expression and MET amplification, biomarkers associated with poor prognosis. Importantly, responses were also observed in patients without these alterations, suggesting broader therapeutic potential. These findings support the clinical relevance of c-Met as a therapeutic target and highlight the feasibility of ADC-based strategies in GEA. The results provide a rationale for further investigation of Temab-A, including in combination regimens, and may inform future biomarker-driven treatment approaches. This study addresses a critical unmet need and contributes to the development of more effective, personalized therapies for patients with advanced GEA.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Gastrointestinal tumors, including esophageal and gastric/gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma (GEA), were diagnosed in approximately 1.4 million patients globally in 2022 (1, 2); gastric cancer was the fifth most common type of malignant tumor and had the fifth highest cancer mortality rate (1, 3). Although worldwide incidence rates for gastric cancer have declined, there is an increased risk in younger people from higher-income countries (2, 4). These patients more frequently present with proximally located tumors, including GEAs, which are associated with worse outcomes compared with distal gastric cancers (5). Most new cases occur in Asia, Eastern/Central Europe, and South America (6, 7). The majority of gastric cancer cases are adenocarcinomas that are often diagnosed at an advanced stage, as patients do not commonly demonstrate clear symptoms in the early stages of the disease (6). This presents challenging and unmet clinical needs in treating these patients.

For patients with advanced GEA, the most common second-line therapy is paclitaxel with or without ramucirumab. In the RAINBOW trial, the combination of paclitaxel and ramucirumab resulted in a median overall survival (OS) of 9.6 months and a median progression-free survival (PFS) of 4.4 months (8). Paclitaxel monotherapy outcomes were inferior to the combination (8), but it remains a standard of care in some countries where ramucirumab is not available or reimbursed. Trifluridine/tipiracil may be offered, but this does not extend the median OS beyond 6 months or the median PFS beyond 2 months (9). With the advances in the field of immunotherapy and targeted therapy in recent decades, combination treatment can now be or is soon to be guided by the expression status of human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), Claudin 18.2 (CLDN18.2), fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2), and programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1; refs. 10–13). However, outcomes for patients with metastatic gastric cancer remain poor, with a 5-year survival rate of 7% (14).

The receptor tyrosine kinase c-Met (also known as MET protein) is encoded by the MET proto-oncogene and has been shown to play a central role in normal cellular processes such as migration, proliferation, and survival. However, the dysregulation of its activity and downstream signaling can promote tumor progression, metastasis, and resistance to therapy (15, 16). Multiple studies have shown that c-Met protein is expressed in numerous types of carcinomas, including breast, lung, ovarian, colorectal, pancreatic, stomach, and GEA (17–25). c-Met protein expression or MET gene focal amplification has been shown to be an indicator of poor prognosis in patients with GEA (26–28), and a recent study found that 65% of gastric carcinoma tissues had c-Met expression, which correlated with poor patient survival (22). Historically, targeting c-Met with tyrosine kinase inhibitors has elicited mixed success and has been associated with resistance to therapy (29, 30).

Telisotuzumab adizutecan (Temab-A, ABBV-400) is a novel antibody–drug conjugate (ADC) comprising the c-Met–targeting antibody telisotuzumab (ABT-700) conjugated to adizutecan, a potent topoisomerase 1 (Top1) inhibitor payload. Temab-A binds to the c-Met protein receptor on the cell surface and delivers the Top1 inhibitor payload, which results in cytotoxic cell death. Temab-A has shown promising results in patients with GEA (31), and an ongoing phase I, first-in-human, multipart trial (NCT05029882) is assessing the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics (PK) of Temab-A treatment in patients with solid tumors whose disease has progressed while on standard cancer therapies. During the dose escalation part of this study, clinical activity was observed, and safety outcomes were comparable with other Top1 inhibitors (32–34). Here, we present the safety, efficacy, and PK results, as well as exploratory biomarker analysis from the dose expansion part of this study in patients with GEA.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This phase I, open-label, multicenter study was designed to assess Temab-A treatment in patients with solid tumors, including nonsquamous non–small cell lung cancer [NSCLC; with wild-type or mutated epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) expression], colorectal cancer, and GEA. Dose escalation determined the maximum tolerated dose/recommended expansion dose to be 3 mg/kg administered intravenously (i.v.) every 3 weeks (Supplementary Fig. S1). For patients with a weight >120 kg, a 120-kg cap was used for dosing calculation. In the dose expansion portion of the study, Temab-A monotherapy (3 mg/kg every 3 weeks i.v.) was evaluated in patients with advanced GEA until disease progression, intolerable toxicity, or withdrawal of consent. Temab-A treatment was discontinued if the patient developed grade 2 or higher treatment-emergent interstitial lung disease (ILD) or pneumonitis.

The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice Guidelines of the International Conference on Harmonization and was approved by regulatory and independent ethics committees/Institutional Review Boards at each site. All patients provided written informed consent before any study procedures were performed.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: Patients ≥18 years of age with advanced or metastatic gastric or GEA not amenable to surgical resection were eligible for the GEA expansion cohort. All patients were required to have measurable disease per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1 (RECIST v1.1) and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1. Patients who had received at least one, but not more than two, prior cytotoxic chemotherapeutic regimens in the setting of locally advanced or metastatic disease were included; as applicable, patients must have also experienced progression on an immune checkpoint inhibitor and/or appropriate available therapies, such as HER2-directed agents. Patients were also eligible if they were considered by the investigator to be ineligible for or have intolerance to standard therapy. Initially, patients were prospectively selected for enrollment on the basis of c-Met expression >90% 1+ cutoff; however, due to more than 80% of prescreened patients meeting this prespecified selection criterion, the prospective selection requirement was removed. Race and ethnicity were self-reported by patients at screening.

Key exclusion criteria included prior treatment with a c-Met protein–targeting antibody or ADC, a history of ILD/pneumonitis requiring systemic steroid treatment, or active ILD/pneumonitis. Additionally, patients were excluded if they had a history of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, organizing pneumonia, drug-induced pneumonitis, or idiopathic pneumonitis.

sec.title: Outcomes and assessments
sec.p: The primary objectives for the dose expansion phase of this study were to assess the safety, efficacy, and PK of Temab-A monotherapy in patients with GEA. Safety endpoints included the monitoring of adverse events (AE; including progressive disease), vital sign measurements, physical examination results, electrocardiogram variables, and clinical laboratory testing. The primary efficacy endpoint was the confirmed objective response rate (ORR), which was defined as the proportion of patients with a confirmed complete response (CR) or partial response (PR), as assessed by the investigator per RECIST v1.1. Additional efficacy endpoints were the duration of response (DOR) for patients with confirmed CR/PR per RECIST v1.1, PFS per RECIST v1.1, and OS. Tumor assessments were performed at baseline and every 6 weeks (corresponding to every two cycles) until cycle 17, and then every 12 weeks until radiographic progression, initiation of new anticancer therapy, death, or consent withdrawal occurred. Serial PK samples were collected, and PK parameters were determined using noncompartmental methods for the Temab-A conjugate, total antibody, and unconjugated Top1 inhibitor payload. These parameters included the maximum observed concentration (Cmax) in serum (or plasma for payload), time to reach Cmax (Tmax), half-life (t1/2), and area under the concentration-time curve for serum (or plasma for payload).

sec.title: Biomarker analysis
sec.p: Tumor tissues, recently obtained (within 6 months) and archival, were collected during prescreening and screening for exploratory biomarker analysis. c-Met protein expression was evaluated retrospectively by immunohistochemistry (IHC) using the clinical trial assay for MET (SP44; Roche Diagnostics, RRID:SCR_025096). c-Met positivity was defined as ≥10% of tumor cells with 3+ staining intensity (≥10%|3+), and in patients with lower c-Met protein expression, it was defined as <10% of tumor cells with 3+ staining intensity (<10%|3+). Whole blood and plasma samples were collected for exploratory biomarker analyses at screening, before the Temab-A dose on dosing day 1 of every cycle, and at the 30-day follow-up for exploratory biomarkers.

Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) from plasma collected at baseline and cycle 3 day 1 was analyzed for ctDNA percent change and molecular response using the Guardant INFINITY assay. MET amplification was determined retrospectively in plasma ctDNA at baseline using the Guardant Infinity panel or reported by sites through a local tissue-based assay. MET amplification by ctDNA was determined using the Guardant gene-specific copy-number threshold versus diploid baseline algorithm [cutoff MET 2.2 or more copy-number variation; ctDNA amplification in which MET is amplified above and beyond nearby genes on the panel (focal); MET amplifications amplified in the context of a larger chromosomal amplification event on the panel (aneuploidy)]. Correlative analyses of c-Met expression with clinical response were performed.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The full analysis set, which included all patients with GEA who received one or more doses of Temab-A, was used for all safety, efficacy, PK, and baseline analyses. PFS was defined as the time from the first Temab-A treatment to documented disease progression per RECIST v1.1 or death due to any cause, whichever occurred earlier. OS was defined as the time from the first Temab-A treatment to death by any cause. The clinical benefit rate (CBR) was the proportion of patients with a confirmed CR, PR, or stable disease. DOR was defined for patients with a confirmed CR/PR as the time from the initial response of CR/PR per investigator review according to RECIST v1.1 criteria to disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurred earlier. ORR/CBR endpoints were presented with two-sided 95% confidence intervals (CI) based on the Clopper–Pearson exact method (35). Kaplan–Meier estimates were used for median DOR, PFS, and OS endpoints, along with their two-sided 95% CI. Statistical comparisons of PK parameters between Asian and non-Asian patients were performed using the Mann–Whitney U test.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: A total of 42 patients with advanced GEA were enrolled in the dose expansion part of the study and received one or more doses of Temab-A as of the data cutoff (September 25, 2024). Of the 42 patients with GEA enrolled, 20 were enrolled using the prospective c-Met selection (>90% 1+ cutoff), and 22 were enrolled in an unselected manner. Patient demographics and baseline disease characteristics are presented in Table 1. The median age was 60 years (range, 28–79); most patients (83%) were male; and 29% (12/42) identified as Asian. The median number of prior systemic therapies was two (range, 1–5). All patients had prior chemotherapy; 26 (62%) had prior checkpoint immunotherapy; and 20 (48%) had prior targeted therapy. The median patient body mass index (BMI) was 22.6 kg/m2 (range, 14.6–40.5), with seven (17%) patients having a BMI <18.5 kg/m2 and five (12%) patients with a BMI ≥30 kg/m2. Baseline characteristics were generally representative of the GEA population (Supplementary Table S1).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: The safety profile of Temab-A in patients with GEA is summarized in Table 3. All patients with GEA experienced one or more treatment-emergent AEs (TEAEs), and 37 (88%) experienced a grade ≥3 TEAE, with the most frequent events being hematologic or gastrointestinal. The most common hematologic TEAEs were anemia (67%), neutropenia (26%), and thrombocytopenia (26%); grade ≥3 hematologic TEAEs occurred in 55% of patients. The most common nonhematologic TEAEs were nausea (52%), decreased appetite (36%), hypoalbuminemia (33%), and constipation (29%); grade ≥3 gastrointestinal events occurred in 14% (n = 6) of patients. The adjudicated ILD/pneumonitis rate was 5%; grade 1 and grade 2 events were observed in one patient each. Anemia occurred in 28 patients, of whom 18 required red blood cell transfusions. Thrombocytopenia occurred in 11 patients, of whom three required platelet transfusions. All cases were managed according to institutional guidelines.

sec.p: TEAEs led to the discontinuation of Temab-A in eight (19%) patients with GEA; these events were small intestinal obstruction (n = 1, grade 3), cholestatic jaundice (n = 1, grade 3), sepsis (n = 1, grade 4), septic shock (n = 1, fatal), malignant neoplasm progression (n = 2, grade 3), and ILD (n = 2; grade 1, n = 1 and grade 2, n = 1). Of these, three (7%) were deemed related to Temab-A (sepsis and ILD). Although dose interruptions and reductions were attributed to hematologic toxicities in 36% and 31% of patients, respectively, no treatment discontinuations due to hematologic toxicity occurred. TEAEs leading to death occurred in 17 (40%) patients, of which 11 (26%) were due to malignant neoplasm progression. Treatment-related AEs leading to death occurred in two (5%) patients, one of which was due to sepsis and one due to sudden death. In addition to the two treatment-related deaths, four other patients experienced TEAEs that led to death. These events included septic shock (n = 1), small intestinal obstruction (n = 1), hepatic failure (n = 1), and ischemic stroke (n = 1).

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: The efficacy data for patients with advanced GEA are shown in Table 4. Overall, the ORR was 29% (95% CI, 16–45), the CBR was 71% (95% CI, 55–84), and the median DOR was 4.2 months (95% CI, 2.7–not estimable). Responses to therapy were seen both in patients who had received one and two or more prior therapies (Fig. 1A and B). Partial responses were also observed in patients who were previously treated with anti-PD–L1 (n = 9/26), anti-VEGF (n = 3/11), and anti-HER2 agents (n = 2/5); the five patients who had prior treatment with a Top1 inhibitor all had a best response of stable disease. Efficacy outcomes were similar among Asian and non-Asian patients (ORR of 33% and 27%, respectively). In the total population, median PFS was 4 months (95% CI, 2.76–4.86) and median OS was 5.82 months (95% CI, 4.96–7.46).

sec.title: PK
sec.p: PK parameters in cycle 1 for patients with GEA are summarized in Supplementary Table S2. PK sampling was conducted during cycle 1 to characterize the concentration-time profiles of the Temab-A conjugate and the released Top1 inhibitor. Peak payload concentrations were observed within 24 hours (median Tmax). The apparent t1/2 of the Temab-A conjugate was approximately 4.4 days and the Top1 inhibitor payload t1/2 was approximately 8.7 days following 3 mg/kg every 3 weeks dosing. The concentration-time profiles for the Temab-A conjugate and Top1 inhibitor payload are shown in Supplementary Fig. S2. PK results were similar among Asian and non-Asian patients and are shown in Supplementary Fig. S3.

sec.title: Biomarker analysis
sec.p: c-Met protein expression was analyzed via IHC in 44 archival and 26 recently obtained tissue samples collected from patients with GEA from the dose escalation and dose expansion parts of the study. ORR was enriched in patients with higher c-Met protein expression (Fig. 2; Supplementary Table S3). MET amplification was detected in 29% of patients either via plasma ctDNA analysis or reports from local sites. A positive correlation was found between response to treatment and MET amplification (Supplementary Fig. S4); due to the limited sample size and exploratory nature of this analysis, any statistical comparisons should be interpreted cautiously. Longitudinal analysis of ctDNA showed a positive correlation between changes in ctDNA levels and changes in tumor volume from baseline (Supplementary Fig. S5).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: GEA remains a highly lethal disease and is one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality globally (1, 3, 36). Several targeted therapies for patients with metastatic GEA are in development; targets include HER2, CLDN18.2, FGFR2, VEGFR2, and PD-L1 inhibitors. VEGF and FGFR2 are under investigation as potential therapeutic targets in gastric and gastroesophageal junction cancers, although they are not yet established as predictive biomarkers. These targeted therapies are promising, but not all GEA tumors express these genes, and therefore new targets such as c-Met, which have been shown to be expressed in up to 65% of gastric carcinoma tissues (22), are currently under investigation.

In the phase III RAINBOW study, combination therapy of VEGFR2 antagonist ramucirumab with paclitaxel in patients with second-line and beyond GEA resulted in a median OS of 9.6 months (8), and pembrolizumab monotherapy demonstrated a median OS of 9.1 months, compared with 8.3 months with paclitaxel monotherapy in patients with PD-L1–positive tumors (Combined Positive Score ≥1; ref. 37). Furthermore, paclitaxel plus ramucirumab demonstrated a median PFS of 4.4 months, whereas paclitaxel and ramucirumab monotherapies yielded PFS of 2.9 and 2.1 months, respectively. In this study, Temab-A monotherapy achieved a median PFS of 3.98 months in patients with advanced GEA treated in the second line and beyond. These findings support further investigation of Temab-A in combination with other agents to potentially enhance clinical benefit in this population.

In the third-line setting, nivolumab demonstrated a median OS of 5.3 months and a median PFS of 1.6 months in the ATTRACTION-2 trial, which enrolled patients with advanced GEA that had progressed after at least two prior regimens (38). The TAGS trial, which evaluated trifluridine–tipiracil in patients with metastatic gastric cancer who had received two or more prior lines of therapy, reported a median OS of 5.7 months and a median PFS of 2 months in heavily pretreated patients (9). The PFS observed with Temab-A monotherapy (4 months) further supports its potential role across later lines of therapy.

Risk factors for GEA include Helicobacter pylori infection, age, dietary factors, obesity (defined as a BMI of more than 30), chronic gastroesophageal reflux, and genetic predispositions (39). Patients with GEA can have complications related to the primary tumor that include bleeding, obstruction, or perforation, and severe malnutrition is common in patients undergoing surgery for gastrointestinal tumors (40). These factors, along with diagnosis often occurring at advanced stages of the disease, contribute to challenges in treating patients with GEA and can lead to worse outcomes. In this study, 17% of the patients with advanced GEA had a BMI <18 kg/m2 at baseline, and patients were overall heavily pretreated, with 50% of patients receiving two or more prior therapies. The impact of BMI on treatment outcomes is crucial (41), as lower BMI can exacerbate the challenges in managing TEAEs and overall patient health. Despite these challenges, no clear association between BMI and toxicity was observed, and Temab-A monotherapy had a manageable safety profile that was consistent with the total study population (34). Additionally, this is consistent with the broader safety profile observed across other Top1 inhibitor ADCs (32, 33), which similarly report frequent hematologic and gastrointestinal AEs. In a phase I study of ABBV-400 (Temab-A) in colorectal cancer, grade ≥3 TEAEs occurred in 71% of patients, with anemia (35%), neutropenia (7%), and febrile neutropenia (6%) being the most common (34). Similarly, trastuzumab deruxtecan, an anti-HER2 ADC with a Top1 payload, was associated with grade ≥3 TEAEs in 55.7% of patients with gastric cancer, including anemia (13.9%), neutrophil count decrease (7.6%), and white blood cell decrease (6.3%; ref. 42). However, these events are typically predictable and can be effectively managed through proactive monitoring, timely dose adjustments, and supportive care measures. In our study, although 88% of patients experienced grade ≥3 TEAEs, no treatment discontinuations occurred due to hematologic toxicity, and the majority of nonhematologic events were low grade. These findings reinforce the importance of vigilant clinical oversight and suggest that, with appropriate management strategies, Temab-A can be safely administered to patients with varying BMI levels.

The relationship between drug exposure and grade ≥ AEs has been previously reported (43, 44). Low rates of immunogenicity have been observed with Temab-A in the phase I trial, including patients with GEA (only one of 42 patients tested positive for antidrug antibodies at a post-baseline measurement; ref. 44). Understanding exposure-response relationships remains an important area for ongoing investigation, particularly as dose optimization and patient selection strategies evolve in subsequent studies.

Temab-A monotherapy showed antitumor activity in patients with advanced GEA, with a median ORR of 29% and a median DOR of 4.2 months. Although these data are encouraging, this study is limited by the patient sample size of 42, and larger studies with patient randomization are needed. Antitumor activity was also observed in heavily treated patients (those with two or more lines of prior therapy), with an ORR of 24% and a median DOR that was not reached. This is notable in the context of a heavily pretreated population, in which therapeutic options are limited and response rates are typically low. Clinical responses to Temab-A were also observed in patients who had previously received various targeted agents, including anti-PD–L1, anti-VEGF, and anti-HER2 therapies. The partial responses reported in patients previously treated with these cancer therapies are clinically relevant as exposure to some of these agents is known to affect tumor biology and may influence c-Met expression (the direct effect of prior anti-PD–L1 therapy on c-Met expression/signaling has not been clearly established; refs. 45, 46). Importantly, responses were observed across both biomarker-selected and -unselected patients, suggesting potential activity beyond predefined MET expression thresholds. Nevertheless, the interpretation of MET as a predictive biomarker remains complex, and variability in detection methods (e.g., IHC assay, cutoff criteria) may influence response outcomes. These factors underscore the need for further validation in larger, controlled studies before advancing to phase III trials.

The observed prevalence of MET amplification in this study, 28.6% (12/42, ctDNA, and local testing), was higher compared with the 2% to 8% reported in the literature (47–49). In exploratory biomarker analyses, ORR enrichment was observed in patients with advanced GEA with MET amplification, although responses to Temab-A were found in patients both with and without MET amplification. Additionally, a positive correlation was found between the change in ctDNA levels and the change in tumor size from baseline. Therapeutic responses were observed in patients with both higher and lower levels of c-Met protein expression. The threshold of c-Met protein expression has not yet been developed to guide the use of c-Met as a predictive biomarker for treatment-related decisions, and analyses are ongoing to determine the association of c-Met expression with treatment response.

Temab-A and telisotuzumab vedotin (Teliso-V) are both c-Met–targeting ADCs that differ in their cytotoxic payloads. Teliso-V utilizes a monomethyl auristatin E payload, whereas ABBV-400 employs a Top1 inhibitor. In the phase II LUMINOSITY trial, Teliso-V demonstrated an ORR of 28.6% in patients with nonsquamous EGFR-wild-type NSCLC, with a higher ORR of 34.6% in the c-Met–high subgroup (50). The median DOR was 8.3 months, and the most common grade ≥3 treatment-related AE was peripheral sensory neuropathy (7%). In contrast, Temab-A demonstrated an ORR of 29% in patients with advanced GEA treated in the second- or third-line setting, with a distinct safety profile characterized primarily by hematologic and gastrointestinal toxicities. These differences may reflect not only the distinct payloads and tumor types but also differences in c-Met expression patterns and detection methods and highlight the importance of optimizing ADC design and patient selection strategies in future clinical development.

This study has several limitations. The small sample size and lack of a control arm limit the generalizability of the findings and preclude definitive conclusions about comparative efficacy. Additionally, heterogeneity in biomarker selection, including variability in c-Met expression assessment, may have influenced response outcomes. Potential selection bias related to MET expression, particularly in the IHC-selected cohort, should also be considered when interpreting the results. It should also be noted that the study population had a relatively favorable prognosis, as reflected by the median time from initial diagnosis to study entry of approximately 1 year. This may have influenced observed outcomes and should be considered when interpreting efficacy results.

In conclusion, this study demonstrated that Temab-A has a manageable safety profile and encouraging antitumor activity in patients with advanced GEA treated in the second- and third-line settings. Ongoing and future studies (e.g., NCT06628310) will further define its role in the treatment landscape, including in biomarker-selected populations and in combination with other agents.

sec.title: Data Availability
sec.p: AbbVie is committed to responsible data sharing about the clinical trials we sponsor. This includes access to anonymized, individual, and trial-level data (analysis datasets), as well as other information (e.g., protocols, clinical study reports, synopses, or statistical analysis plans), as long as the trials are not part of an ongoing or planned regulatory submission. These clinical trial data can be requested by any qualified researchers who engage in rigorous, independent scientific research and will be provided following the review and approval of a research proposal, Statistical Analysis Plan, and execution of a Data Use Agreement. Data requests can be submitted at any time after approval in the United States and Europe and after acceptance of this manuscript for publication. sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: AbbVie is committed to responsible data sharing about the clinical trials we sponsor. This includes access to anonymized, individual, and trial-level data (analysis datasets), as well as other information (e.g., protocols, clinical study reports, synopses, or statistical analysis plans), as long as the trials are not part of an ongoing or planned regulatory submission. These clinical trial data can be requested by any qualified researchers who engage in rigorous, independent scientific research and will be provided following the review and approval of a research proposal, Statistical Analysis Plan, and execution of a Data Use Agreement. Data requests can be submitted at any time after approval in the United States and Europe and after acceptance of this manuscript for publication. For more information on the process or to submit a request, visit the following link: https://vivli.org/ourmember/abbvie/ and then select “Home.”
